questions.q: What is the primary purpose of "evidence-based discussion" in the context of analyzing a literary text like "oqQVt"?
questions.a: The primary purpose is to ground interpretations in specific textual details (words, phrases, structural choices) so that claims about theme, character, or philosophy can be verified, challenged, or refined by all participants using the same shared source. A wrong answer like "to express personal feelings about the story" reveals the student confuses discussion with opinion-sharing — they haven't grasped that literary discussion requires accountability to the text, not just subjective reaction.

questions.a: The distinction means ":i" (form/essence) is who a person truly is — their inner self, consciousness, unique being — while "uke" (name) is the label society assigns: caste, profession, family role, legal identity. questions.q: Apply the "State-Quote-Explain-Invite" discussion cycle to this claim: "The author suggests that true home (oqQVt) is not a physical house but a state of being." Use a specific textual reference from pages 133-135.
questions.a: State: True home is existential, not architectural. Quote: Page 134 — "oqQVt vFkkZr tks oqQV ls iSnk gqvk gksA ... iwQy xeys esa gksrs vo'; gSa] ij oqQVt rks taxy dk lSykuh gSA" (Home is what is born from house... walls are in houses, but home is the essence of journey). Explain: The author separates physical structure (walls, roof) from the lived experience of belonging — home travels with you as "taxy dk lSykuh" (essence of journey). Invite: "Does anyone see a counter-example where physical space anchors identity?" A wrong answer that quotes only the Sanskrit etymology ("oqQfVgkfjdk") shows the student can retrieve facts but cannot synthesize them into an argument — they're doing retrieval, not discussion.

questions.q: Compare how the concept of "thuk" (thirst/longing) functions on page 135 ("thuk Hkh ,d dyk gS... ysfdu dyk gh ugha] riL;k gS") with its function in the Sanskrit verse on page 136 ("ân;sukijkftr%! fdruk fo'kky og ân; gksxk tks lq[k ls, nq[k ls, fiz; ls, vfiz; ls fopkyr u gksrk gksxk"). What does this comparison reveal about the author's philosophical progression?
questions.a: On page 135, "thuk" is human longing — creative, artistic, a discipline ("riL;k") that drives self-transcendence. By page 136, the Sanskrit verse elevates it to a cosmic principle: the ultimate reality ("ân;") is that which cannot be touched by pleasure/pain, virtue/vice. The progression moves from individual psychology to metaphysical ontology — longing becomes the bridge between finite human experience and infinite truth. A wrong answer that says "both mean the same thing" reveals the student cannot track conceptual development across the text — they treat each passage in isolation instead of analyzing the argument's architecture.

questions.q: Evaluate this student claim: "The author romanticizes poverty and suffering in 'oqQVt' — he makes the village road's darkness sound beautiful." Defend or refute using textual evidence.
questions.a: Refute. The text explicitly rejects romanticization: page 131 — "laiw.kZ fgeky; dks ns[kdj gh fdlh osQ eu esa lekfèkLFk egknso dh ewfrZ Li"V gqbZ gksxh" (seeing the real village, a strange pride awakens in anyone's heart) — "ewfrZ" (pride) not pity. And page 135: "nqjar thou&'kfDr gSA dfBu mins'k gSA" (intense life-experience. Rare purpose.) The author frames suffering as revelatory, not aesthetic. A wrong answer that agrees with the claim reveals the student confuses vivid description with glorification — they haven't learned to distinguish tone (witnessing) from stance (endorsing).

questions.q: Create a 2-minute discussion opening for a peer group on the question: "Can a person have multiple 'oqQVt' (homes) simultaneously?" Your opening must use the State-Quote-Explain-Invite cycle and reference at least two different pages.
questions.a: [Sample strong opening] State: Yes, the text supports multiple simultaneous homes — physical, linguistic, and existential. Quote 1: Page 134 — "laLÑr loZxzklh Hkk"kk gSA" (Sanskrit is universal language) — language as portable home. Quote 2: Page 136 — "euq"; th jgk gS] osQoy th jgk gS_ viuh bPNk ls ugha] bfrgkl&foèkkrk dh ;kstuk osQ vuqlkj" (The Beloved alone exists... not from your side, but by history-design's plan) — spiritual home transcends geography. Explain: Home isn't singular location but layered belonging — mother tongue, memory, consciousness. Invite: "Where in the text does the author suggest we must choose ONLY one?" A weak opening that only gives personal opinion ("I think we have many homes") without textual anchors reveals the student hasn't internalized evidence-based discussion protocol.
